kurals.tamil:
கைம்மாறு வேண்டா கடப்பாடு மாரிமாட்டு
என்ஆற்றுங் கொல்லோ உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaimmaaru vendaa kadappaadu maarimaattu
En aatrung kollo ulagu.
kurals.meaning: True duty toward others does not look for anything in return. After all, what does the world ever give back to the rain-cloud that waters it?
kurals.elementary: The rain falls on everyone's fields and never sends a bill. Nobody pays the clouds back, and the clouds never ask. This kural says good people help others the same way — just because it is right, not to get something back.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter by naming the virtue kadappaadu — literally ‘what is owed, what cannot be set aside’ — and then startles the reader by saying this obligation expects no repayment. The rhetorical question (en aatrum kollo, ‘what does it do?’) is read by Parimelazhagar as an emphatic ‘nothing at all’: living beings return nothing to the clouds, so those who resemble clouds do not calculate returns either. Manakkudavar glosses kadappaadu directly as oppuravu, defining it as giving suited to one's means to the deserving without seeking recompense. The image deliberately recalls Chapter 2 (Vaan Sirappu, the Excellence of Rain), turning a cosmological fact into an ethical model: the benefactor is a natural force of sustenance, not a party to a contract. The paradox — a duty that is binding yet unrepaid — anticipates later debates about whether generosity can be obligatory without becoming exchange.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, without being attached to the fruits of activities, one should act as a matter of duty, for by working without attachment one attains the Supreme.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna to do what is right because it is his duty, not because of what he will get out of it.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's kadappaadu, duty here is binding precisely because it ignores any reward.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on reward-free duty; the Gita speaks of action generally, not specifically of helping others, and lacks the rain image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his followers to do good and lend without expecting to be paid back, imitating God who is kind even to the ungrateful.
christianity.tie_back: Same ethic of giving that ‘hopes for nothing again,’ modeled on a divine generosity that, like rain, falls on all.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on non-reciprocal giving; Luke adds a heavenly reward the Kural does not mention.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Saying], ‘We feed you only for the countenance of Allah. We wish not from you reward or gratitude.’”
islam.explanation: The righteous who feed the poor, orphan, and captive say they want neither payment nor even thanks from the people they help.
islam.tie_back: Mirrors the Kural's cloud that asks nothing back — not even gratitude — from those it nourishes.
islam._accuracy_note: Near-exact match on giving without seeking return; the motive is explicitly God's pleasure.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Do not be like servants who serve the master in the expectation of receiving a reward, but be like servants who serve the master without the expectation of receiving a reward, and let the fear of Heaven be upon you.”
judaism.explanation: Antigonus of Socho teaches that right action should be done for its own sake, not for a payoff.
judaism.tie_back: Shares the Kural's insistence that genuine duty does not bargain for recompense.
judaism._accuracy_note: Same reward-free principle; the saying concerns service of God rather than service to society.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A person responsive to requests, sympathetic to all beings, delighting in distributing alms ... As a cloud—resounding, thundering—rains, filling with water, drenching the plateaus & gullies: a person like this is like that.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha sorts people into three kinds: a cloud that never rains, one that rains only in some places, and one that rains everywhere. The best giver is like the cloud that soaks the whole land.
buddhism.tie_back: Uses the very same rain-cloud image as the Kural to describe the ideal, all-embracing benefactor.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Remarkable parallel: identical metaphor of the generous person as a rain-cloud serving all.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Demeter gives Triptolemus a chariot drawn by winged dragons and wheat, with which he travels the inhabited earth sowing grain for all humankind.
greek_mythology.explanation: In myth, the gift of agriculture is spread freely across the world by the goddess's messenger.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like rain, the gift of grain is given to everyone, and no one repays Demeter in kind.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best match: a divine gift of sustenance to all, but Greek religion did expect sacrifices to the gods in return, unlike the Kural's cloud.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “the immortal gods ... help all alike, among them even those who so ill appreciate their bounty. Let us take them for our guides as far as the weakness of our mortal nature permits; let us bestow benefits, not put them out at interest.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that people should give like the gods, who help everyone, even the ungrateful, rather than treating gifts as loans that earn interest.
philosophy.tie_back: Same model: the benefactor imitates a universal, unpaid bounty, as the Kural's rain does.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close in logic; Seneca elsewhere discusses the recipient's duty of gratitude, which the Kural leaves aside.

kurals.tamil:
தாளாற்றித் தந்த பொருளெல்லாம் தக்கார்க்கு
வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Thaalaatrith thandha porulellaam thakkaarkku
Velaanmai seydhar poruttu.
kurals.meaning: All the wealth a person earns through hard, persistent effort exists for one purpose: to be used in helping those who deserve help.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you worked all summer and saved up money. This kural says the best reason to work hard and earn is so that you have something to share with people who really need it.
kurals.university: The first line honours effort (thaal aatri, ‘exerting one's foot/strength’), so the kural is not a critique of wealth but a statement of its telos. Velaanmai here does not mean agriculture but ubakaram, beneficence — Parimelazhagar glosses it as oppuravu seydhal, adding that wealth is not meant for eating alone or for hoarding until it is lost. Thakkaar, ‘the worthy,’ introduces discernment: Manakkudavar defines oppuravu as giving to fitting recipients in proportion to one's income, which distinguishes it from the indiscriminate almsgiving of the next chapter (Eekai). The couplet thus rejects both the miser and the ascetic view of wealth, proposing instead a stewardship model in which earnings are held in trust for the community.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Charity given out of duty, without expectation of return, at the proper time and place, and to a worthy person is considered to be in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the highest kind of charity: given as a duty, at the right time and place, to someone who deserves it.
hinduism.tie_back: Matches the Kural's thakkaar (the worthy) and its sense that giving is the proper use of what one has.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on giving to the worthy as duty; the Gita does not stress that wealth is earned by one's own toil.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to work honestly so that they will have something to give to people in need.
christianity.tie_back: Almost the same logic: the purpose of one's labour is to be able to help others.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match of labour-for-giving; Paul says ‘him that needeth’ where the Kural says ‘the worthy.’

islam.quote_or_event: “Believe in Allah and His Messenger and spend out of that in which He has made you successors. For those who have believed among you and spent, there will be a great reward.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents wealth as a trust from God, which believers are to spend for good.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, wealth is not simply owned but held for the purpose of beneficial spending.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the stewardship idea; frames wealth as God-entrusted rather than self-earned, and promises reward.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For the poor shall never cease out of the land: therefore I command thee, saying, Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy brother, to thy poor, and to thy needy, in thy land.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah commands generosity as a permanent duty, since need will always exist in society.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes helping others the proper, commanded use of one's means.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on duty to share; lacks the Kural's point about wealth gained by effort being for this purpose.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “the disciple of the noble ones — using the wealth earned through his efforts & enterprise, amassed through the strength of his arm, and piled up through the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained — provides his friends & associates with pleasure & satisfaction, and maintains that pleasure rightly.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the good uses of honestly earned wealth, including supporting friends, relatives, guests, and the virtuous.
buddhism.tie_back: Echoes the Kural's ‘wealth earned by effort’ and its purpose of benefiting others.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.41, Adiya Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on effort-earned wealth used for others; the sutta also includes self-enjoyment, which the Kural omits.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Give to one who gives, but do not give to one who does not give. A man gives to the free-handed, but no one gives to the close-fisted. Give is a good girl, but Take is bad and she brings death.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's farmer's wisdom praises giving but ties it to reciprocity among neighbours.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shares the Kural's praise of giving and its concern with choosing recipients, but grounds it in exchange rather than duty.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 352–369 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Partial and contrasting: Hesiod's selectivity is based on return, while the Kural's thakkaar is about worthiness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “the liberal man, like other virtuous men, will give for the sake of the noble, and rightly; for he will give to the right people, the right amounts, and at the right time, with all the other qualifications that accompany right giving”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle describes the virtue of liberality: using wealth well by giving it rightly to the right people.
philosophy.tie_back: Same idea as the Kural's velaanmai to the thakkaar — wealth's proper use is fitting generosity.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong structural match; Aristotle frames it as a mean between prodigality and meanness.

kurals.tamil:
புத்தே ளுலகத்தும் ஈண்டும் பெறலரிதே
ஒப்புரவின் நல்ல பிற.
kurals.transliteration:
Puththe lulagaththum eendum peralaridhe
Oppuravin nalla pira.
kurals.meaning: Neither in the world of the gods nor here on earth is it easy to find any other good equal to helping others as the world rightly expects.
kurals.elementary: If you searched every place — here and even up in heaven — for the very best thing a person can do, you would find nothing better than helping others. It is the top prize of all good deeds.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar gives an ingenious reason for why oppuravu is rare even in heaven: in the world of the gods all are equal, so there are neither givers nor receivers and the virtue cannot be practised; on earth nothing else benefits everyone so equally. He also records a variant reading, peRaRkaridhu, which some commentators took to mean ‘the means to obtain it is rare.’ With 211 and 212, he notes, this couplet completes the chapter's praise of oppuravu before Valluvar turns to its practice. The comparison of heaven and earth is a recurring Tamil device (cf. Kural 23) for asserting a value's absolute primacy, here placing social beneficence above ritual or ascetic merit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who are beyond the dualities that arise from doubts, whose minds are engaged within, who are always busy working for the welfare of all living beings and who are free from all sins achieve liberation in the Supreme.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names working for the good of all beings (sarva-bhuta-hite ratah) as a mark of those who reach the highest spiritual goal.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks devotion to the welfare of all among the highest goods, reaching beyond this world.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good match on universal welfare as supreme; the Gita links it to liberation and inner discipline.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.”
christianity.explanation: Paul ranks love (charity) above even faith and hope as the greatest virtue.
christianity.tie_back: Same move of ranking love-in-action above all other goods, as the Kural ranks oppuravu.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in ranking structure; Pauline agape is broader than the Kural's socially fitting beneficence.

islam.quote_or_event: “Never will you attain the good [reward] until you spend [in the way of Allah] from that which you love. And whatever you spend - indeed, Allah is Knowing of it.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says true righteousness (al-birr) is not reached until one gives away what one values.
islam.tie_back: Makes generous giving the gateway to the highest good, as the Kural does.
islam._accuracy_note: Similar in making giving essential to the highest good; does not compare heaven and earth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “the world stands upon three things: the Torah, the Temple service, and the practice of acts of piety.”
judaism.explanation: Simeon the Just names gemilut chasadim — acts of loving-kindness — as one of the three pillars holding up the world.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats kindness to others as foundational to the world, not optional.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match; the Mishnah lists it alongside Torah and worship rather than above them.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, if beings knew, as I know, the results of giving & sharing, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of selfishness overcome their minds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that if people understood how great the fruit of sharing is, they would never eat without sharing first, even their last bite.
buddhism.tie_back: Shares the Kural's claim that the good of sharing is unmatched, in this world and after.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on the supreme value of sharing; framed in terms of karmic fruit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Stranger, though a still poorer man should come here, it would not be right for me to insult him, for all strangers and beggars are from Jove.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Eumaeus the swineherd explains that care for strangers and beggars is sacred because Zeus himself protects them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Places helping the needy under divine sanction, echoing the Kural's heaven-and-earth esteem for oppuravu.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best: shows the sacredness of aid, but does not claim it is the highest good of all.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “we are not born for ourselves alone, but our country claims a share of our being, and our friends a share; and since, as the Stoics hold, everything that the earth produces is created for man's use; and as men, too, are born for the sake of men, that they may be able mutually to help one another”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero, citing Plato and the Stoics, argues that humans exist partly for one another and should strengthen society through exchanging kindnesses.
philosophy.tie_back: Articulates the same civic-reciprocity ideal the Kural calls oppuravu and places at the summit of virtue.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis I.22 (trans. Walter Miller)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Excellent match on the social-reciprocity concept itself; Cicero does not rank it against heaven.

kurals.tamil:
ஒத்த தறிவான் உயிர்வாழ்வான் மற்றையான்
செத்தாருள் வைக்கப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Oththa tharivaan uyirvaazhvaan matraiyaan
Seththaarul vaikkap padum.
kurals.meaning: Only the person who understands what is fitting toward the world, and acts on it, is truly alive; anyone else, though breathing, is counted among the dead.
kurals.elementary: A person who never helps anyone is like a statue — they are there, but they do not really take part in life. This kural says being truly alive means knowing how to help the people around you.
kurals.university: The text reproduced here follows the reading ஒத்த தறிவான் (oththadhu arivaan, ‘one who knows what is fitting’) given with Parimelazhagar's commentary; some modern editions print ஒத்த தறவோன் (‘one of fitting virtue’), a variant worth noting. Parimelazhagar glosses oththadhu as ulaga nadai, ‘the conduct of the world,’ and explains that a person who lacks its knowledge and practice shows no sign of the soul's intelligence and action, and so is reckoned dead. He adds a striking remark: a lapse in worldly conduct, unlike a lapse in Vedic rite, has no expiation. The kural thus defines life socially rather than biologically — a theme with parallels from Aristotle's political animal to rabbinic sayings about the ‘living dead.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: “My dear Arjuna, one who does not follow in human life the cycle of sacrifice thus established by the Vedas certainly leads a life full of sin. Living only for the satisfaction of the senses, such a person lives in vain.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that someone who takes from the cosmic cycle of giving without taking part in it lives a wasted life.
hinduism.tie_back: Same verdict as the Kural: a life that ignores reciprocal duty is not really lived (mogham jivati, ‘lives in vain’).
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close — both deny real life to those who refuse the cycle of mutual giving; Gita frames it as yajna.

christianity.quote_or_event: “We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren. He that loveth not his brother abideth in death.”
christianity.explanation: John says that love for others is the sign of real life, and lack of love is a kind of death.
christianity.tie_back: Same life/death contrast defined by one's relationship to others.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on the metaphor; John's ‘love of the brethren’ is community-focused love rather than civic beneficence.

islam.quote_or_event: “None of you will have faith till he wishes for his (Muslim) brother what he likes for himself.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that faith is incomplete without genuinely wanting good for others as for oneself.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes regard for others the test of whether one's inner life is real.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial: shares the social test of true being, but lacks the ‘living dead’ image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “These are the wicked, who even during their lives are called dead”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud teaches that the righteous are called living even after death, while the wicked are called dead even while alive.
judaism.tie_back: Uses the same paradox as the Kural: moral failure makes a living person count as dead.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 18b (Sefaria, William Davidson ed.)
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-identical metaphor; the Talmud's criterion is wickedness in general, not specifically failure to help.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Among the dead they do not die, those who, like fellow travelers on the road, are happy to provide, though they have but little. This is an ancient teaching.”
buddhism.explanation: A deity tells the Buddha that those who share even when they have little do not die among the dead.
buddhism.tie_back: Strikingly parallel: generosity is what separates the truly living from the dead.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 1.32, Macchari Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Remarkable match on both metaphor and cause (sharing); spoken by a deity and approved by the Buddha.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “They have no laws nor assemblies of the people, but live in caves on the tops of high mountains; each is lord and master in his family, and they take no account of their neighbours.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus describes the Cyclopes as monstrous precisely because they live without community or care for neighbours.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Presents those who ignore social obligation as less than human — a mythic version of the Kural's verdict.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Thematic match: the unsocial as sub-human rather than dead.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “he who is unable to live in society, or who has no need because he is sufficient for himself, must be either a beast or a god: he is no part of a state.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that humans are by nature political animals; one who stands outside the shared life of the community is not fully human.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it defines real human life by participation in the community.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual match (zoon politikon); uses beast/god instead of living/dead.

kurals.tamil:
ஊருணி நீர்நிறைந் தற்றே உலகவாம்
பேரறி வாளன் திரு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ooruni neernirain thatre ulagavaam
Perari vaalan thiru.
kurals.meaning: The wealth of a truly wise person who loves to act for the world's good is like the village drinking-pond filled to the brim — there for everyone to draw from.
kurals.elementary: Think of a big water tank in the middle of a village that everyone fills their pots from. When a wise, kind person becomes rich, their money is like that full tank: the whole village benefits.
kurals.university: Ooruni is specifically the common tank from which a village draws its drinking water, a piece of shared infrastructure in Tamil rural life. Parimelazhagar notes the figure of speech — ‘filling’ really belongs to the water but is attributed to the tank — and explains the point: such wealth does not go to waste but lasts long and unfailingly supplies everyone's needs. Ulagu avaam (‘desiring the world’) is read by Parimelazhagar as loving and practising ulaga nadai, while Manakkudavar reads it as ‘desired by the whole world.’ The kural begins a triad (215-217) of public-good images — tank, fruit tree, medicinal tree — that together treat private wealth in virtuous hands as a quasi-public resource.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The riches of the liberal never waste away, while he who will not give finds none to comfort him.”
hinduism.explanation: The Rig Veda's hymn on liberality says generous wealth never runs dry, while the miser ends up alone.
hinduism.tie_back: Echoes Parimelazhagar's point that the generous person's wealth, like the village tank, does not go to waste.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.1 (trans. R. T. H. Griffith)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close match on unfailing generous wealth; lacks the public-tank image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But by an equality, that now at this time your abundance may be a supply for their want, that their abundance also may be a supply for your want: that there may be equality”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks one community to share its surplus with another in need, so that resources flow where they are needed.
christianity.tie_back: Like the full tank, one person's abundance becomes the supply for others' needs.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on abundance as communal supply; Paul adds mutual reciprocity between communities.

islam.quote_or_event: “And from their properties was [given] the right of the [needy] petitioner and the deprived.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes the righteous as those whose wealth contained a rightful share (haqq) for the poor.
islam.tie_back: Treats private wealth as carrying a public claim, as the Kural's tank belongs to the whole village.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on the social right in wealth; no water-tank image.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs promises that the generous person, who ‘waters’ others, will be refreshed in turn.
judaism.tie_back: Shares the water imagery and the idea that generous wealth keeps on supplying.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matching water metaphor; Proverbs emphasises reward to the giver, the Kural the benefit to the village.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Planters of parks or groves, those who build a bridge, a drinking place and well, and those who give monastic quarters. Their merit always grows by day and by night.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha praises those who build public goods — wells, drinking places, bridges, groves — for the whole community.
buddhism.tie_back: Names the very kind of public water source the Kural uses as its image of virtuous wealth.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 1.47, Vanaropa Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on public-works generosity including wells; framed in terms of merit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “A bad neighbour is as great a plague as a good one is a great blessing; he who enjoys a good neighbour has a precious possession.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod advises that a good neighbour is one of the most valuable things a person can have.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Recognises, like the Kural, that a good person's resources are a blessing for the whole neighbourhood.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 342–351 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Partial: neighbourly benefit in general, not wealth as a public resource.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is clearly better that property should be private, but the use of it common; and the special business of the legislator is to create in men this benevolent disposition.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that property should be owned privately, but good people should let it be used for the common benefit.
philosophy.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's model: privately held wealth that functions like the village's common tank.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close structural parallel; Aristotle frames it as a legislative goal.

kurals.tamil:
பயன்மரம் உள்ளூர்ப் பழுத்தற்றால் செல்வம்
நயனுடை யான்கண் படின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Payanmaram ulloorp pazhuththatraal selvam
Nayanudai yaankan padin.
kurals.meaning: When wealth comes to a generous, kindly person, it is like a fruit-bearing tree ripening right in the middle of the village, where everyone can pick its fruit.
kurals.elementary: A fruit tree deep in a forest helps almost no one, but a mango tree in the middle of town feeds everyone who walks by. A kind person's money is like that town tree.
kurals.university: The emphasis falls on ul-oor, ‘inside the village’: the same fruit tree in a distant forest would be of little use, so location stands for accessibility. Parimelazhagar explains nayan (courtesy, kindly propriety) as oppuravu itself, ‘since among the many forms of worldly justice oppuravu is pre-eminent,’ and says the point is that such wealth yields benefit easily to all. Manakkudavar reads nayanudaiyaan as ‘one who is loved by others’ and adds that such wealth benefits even those who dislike him. The couplet moves beyond the tank of 215 to an image of organic, seasonal abundance, suggesting that generosity in the right person is as natural as ripening.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Bounteous is he who gives unto the beggar who comes to him in want of food and feeble. Success attends him in the shout of battle. He makes a friend of him in future troubles.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic hymn praises the giver who feeds the needy, saying such generosity creates lasting bonds.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the village fruit tree, the bountiful person's wealth is open to whoever comes in need.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.3 (trans. R. T. H. Griffith)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good match on accessible generosity; no tree image and adds a practical benefit to the giver.

christianity.quote_or_event: “As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges believers to do good to everyone whenever they get the chance.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural's ideal that a good person's resources should be open to all.
christianity._accuracy_note: Thematic match on doing good to all; no image of wealth-as-tree, and Paul prioritises fellow believers.

islam.quote_or_event: “There is none amongst the Muslims who plants a tree or sows seeds, and then a bird, or a person or an animal eats from it, but is regarded as a charitable gift for him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says that whenever anyone — even an animal — eats from a tree you planted, it counts as charity from you.
islam.tie_back: Uses the same image of a fruit tree whose produce benefits all comers.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong image match; the hadith is about planting as charity, not wealth in a generous person's hands.

judaism.quote_or_event: “That man himself found a world full of carob trees. Just as my ancestors planted for me, I too am planting for my descendants.”
judaism.explanation: A man planting a carob tree that will take seventy years to bear fruit tells Honi he is planting for future generations, as others once did for him.
judaism.tie_back: Presents the fruit tree as a shared gift to the community across time, as in the Kural.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a (Sefaria, William Davidson ed.)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on communal fruit-tree and paying it forward; emphasis is intergenerational rather than on a generous rich person.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One who gives, who is a master of giving, is dear & charming to people at large.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells General Siha that one visible fruit of generosity is being loved by people in general.
buddhism.tie_back: Matches Manakkudavar's reading of nayanudaiyaan as ‘one loved by others’ — the generous person is the village's beloved tree.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.34, Siha Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on the generous person as beloved by the community; no tree image.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the contest for Athens, Athena plants the first olive tree on the Acropolis as her gift to the city, and the city is awarded to her.
greek_mythology.explanation: The olive, giving fruit, oil, and wood to the whole city, was remembered as Athena's great public gift.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A fruit tree planted at the heart of the city for everyone's benefit — close to the Kural's image.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong image parallel (civic fruit tree); the myth concerns divine patronage rather than a generous human's wealth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “he is like a vine which has produced grapes, and seeks for nothing more after it has once produced its proper fruit ... so a man when he has done a good act, does not call out for others to come and see, but he goes on to another act, as a vine goes on to produce again the grapes in season.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius compares the good person to a vine that simply bears fruit, season after season, without seeking credit.
philosophy.tie_back: Same fruit-bearing image for the good person whose benefits flow naturally to others.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close metaphor; Marcus stresses lack of self-regard, the Kural stresses public accessibility.

kurals.tamil:
மருந்தாகித் தப்பா மரத்தற்றால் செல்வம்
பெருந்தகை யான்கண் படின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Marundhaagith thappaa maraththatraal selvam
Perundhagai yaankan padin.
kurals.meaning: When wealth rests with a person of great nobility, it is like a medicinal tree that never fails to heal — every part of it serving as a cure for others.
kurals.elementary: Some trees, like the neem tree, can be used as medicine — the leaves, the bark, even the roots. A great-hearted person's money is like that tree: every part of it helps someone feel better.
kurals.university: Parimelazhagar spells out what thappaa (‘not failing’) excludes: a tree fails if it grows where it is hard to reach, if it is hidden, if it bears only in some seasons, or if it is useless — so the ideal benefactor is accessible, open, reliable, and helpful in every part. He adds that such a person relieves everyone's distress without regard to his own lack. Manakkudavar glosses thapputhal as ‘hiding’: the medicinal tree does not conceal itself from those who seek it. With this third image Parimelazhagar closes the triad on how the benefactor's wealth is used, escalating from water (sustenance) to fruit (nourishment) to medicine (healing).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Just see how these trees are maintaining every living entity! Their birth is successful. Their behavior is just like that of great personalities, for anyone who asks anything from a tree never goes away disappointed.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna praises trees for supporting all creatures, comparing them to great souls who never send a seeker away empty-handed.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost the Kural's image in reverse: the tree is like a great person, just as the great person's wealth is like the tree.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: the unfailing, all-serving tree compared to the great-hearted (perundhagai).

christianity.quote_or_event: “and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.”
christianity.explanation: In John's vision of the new Jerusalem, the tree of life bears fruit every month and its leaves heal the nations.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the image of a tree whose parts are medicine for all people.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong image match; eschatological rather than about a generous person's wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: “Have you not considered how Allah presents an example, [making] a good word like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and its branches [high] in the sky? It produces its fruit all the time, by permission of its Lord.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an compares a good word to a firmly rooted tree that yields fruit at all times.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's thappaa maram, the good tree never fails to give.
islam._accuracy_note: Image of an unfailing tree matches; the referent is a good word (faith), not wealth or healing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “and the fruit thereof shall be for meat, and the leaf thereof for medicine.”
judaism.explanation: Ezekiel foresees trees along a sacred river whose fruit feeds and whose leaves heal.
judaism.tie_back: Shares the Kural's image of a tree whose parts serve as food and medicine for others.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close image; prophetic vision rather than ethical teaching about the wealthy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “For all those ailing in the world, Until their every sickness has been healed, May I myself become for them The doctor, nurse, the medicine itself.”
buddhism.explanation: Shantideva's bodhisattva vows to become the very medicine that cures the world's sick.
buddhism.tie_back: Same idea as the Kural: the great-hearted person becomes medicine for all.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Striking match on ‘becoming medicine’; translation wording varies across editions.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Chiron, the wise centaur renowned for his skill in healing, taught medicine to Asclepius; when wounded incurably by Heracles' arrow, he gave up his immortality, which passed to Prometheus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Chiron is the mythic healer-teacher whose knowledge benefited humanity through his pupils, and who finally gave away even his immortality.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A noble figure whose whole being serves healing, close to the Kural's medicinal tree.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best: healing and self-giving, but not about wealth used for the community.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “no physician, in so far as he is a physician, considers his own good in what he prescribes, but the good of his patient”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues that a true art, like medicine, serves the good of those it cares for, not the practitioner's own gain.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's healing tree, true skill or wealth exists for the benefit of others.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good conceptual match on healing for others' sake; set in an argument about justice and rule.

kurals.tamil:
இடனில் பருவத்தும் ஒப்புரவிற்கு ஒல்கார்
கடனறி காட்சி யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Idanil paruvaththum oppuravirku olkaar
Kadanari kaatchi yavar.
kurals.meaning: Those with a clear understanding of their duty do not slacken in helping others, even when their own means have shrunk.
kurals.elementary: Even when you have only one cookie left, you can still break it in half for a friend. This kural says people who truly understand duty keep helping, even when they do not have much.
kurals.university: Idan il paruvam, literally ‘a season without room,’ refers to a time when wealth has contracted; Parimelazhagar glosses it as selvam surungiya kaalam. Kadan ari kaatchi — ‘the vision that knows what is owed’ — is described by him as natural discernment of what one ought to do, so that even when everything else is given up, this is not. Manakkudavar makes the practical point that oppuravu must be done even when wealth is not abundant. Together with 219, this couplet (Parimelazhagar notes) argues that poverty is no reason to abandon oppuravu, moving the virtue from a function of surplus to a function of character.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Rantideva, after fasting for forty-eight days, gives away the food and water he finally receives to a brahmana, a shudra, a man with dogs, and an outcaste, keeping nothing for himself.
hinduism.explanation: In the Bhagavata Purana, Rantideva, reduced to poverty and hunger, still gives his last food and drink to whoever asks.
hinduism.tie_back: An exact narrative illustration of not slackening in beneficence even in extreme want.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-perfect illustration of giving when one's means are exhausted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus praises a poor widow who gave two small coins — everything she had — above the rich who gave from surplus.
christianity.tie_back: Same lesson: true generosity continues even when one's means are nearly gone.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close match on giving in scarcity.

islam.quote_or_event: “but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul - it is those who will be the successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises the Ansar of Medina who put the needs of the emigrants before their own even while they themselves were poor.
islam.tie_back: Directly matches the Kural's ‘even in a season without means.’
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on giving despite privation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “even a poor person who is sustained from charity must also perform charity.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud rules that even someone who lives on charity is still obligated to give charity to others.
judaism.tie_back: Same principle: lack of means does not cancel the duty to help.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 7b (Sefaria, William Davidson ed.)
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close legal parallel to the Kural's ethic.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Some who have little are happy to provide, while some who have much don't wish to give. An offering given from little is multiplied a thousand times.”
buddhism.explanation: A deity tells the Buddha that giving from little is worth far more than giving from plenty.
buddhism.tie_back: Affirms the Kural's praise for those who keep giving when their means are small.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 1.32, Macchari Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the value of giving from scarcity.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “we have not many spare cloaks nor shirts up here, but every man has only one.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Eumaeus the poor swineherd, with barely enough for himself, still kills his best pig for the disguised Odysseus and covers him with his own heavy cloak for the night.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A poor man who does not slacken in hospitality despite having little — the Kural's ideal.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match; framed as hospitality (xenia) rather than civic beneficence.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “liberality resides not in the multitude of the gifts but in the state of character of the giver, and this is relative to the giver's substance. There is therefore nothing to prevent the man who gives less from being the more liberal man, if he has less to give.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that generosity is measured by character and proportion to one's means, not by the size of the gift.
philosophy.tie_back: Supports the Kural's claim that the dutiful stay generous even when their means are small.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close on generosity relative to means.

kurals.tamil:
நயனுடையான் நல்கூர்ந்தா னாதல் செயும்நீர
செய்யாது அமைகலா வாறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Nayanudaiyaan nalkoorndhaa naadhal seyumneera
Seyyaadhu amaigalaa vaaru.
kurals.meaning: For a kind-hearted person, being ‘poor’ means only one thing: the pain of not being able to do the good deeds he always does.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a kid who loves sharing snacks with everyone. If one day there are no snacks to share, the kid feels sad — not because they are hungry, but because they cannot give. That sadness is what ‘being poor’ means to a kind person.
kurals.university: Valluvar redefines poverty (nalkooral) from the benefactor's point of view: it is not the loss of personal comforts but the anguish of being unable to perform the benefactions that are his nature (seyum neera). Parimelazhagar underlines this: poverty for such a person is ‘not the inability to enjoy what he would enjoy.’ The verb amaigalaa (‘cannot rest content’) captures a moral restlessness, turning the absence of means into a spiritual rather than material deprivation. Paired with 218, the couplet completes Parimelazhagar's point that oppuravu is not to be abandoned because of want.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “I do not pray to the Supreme Personality of Godhead for the eight perfections of mystic yoga, nor for salvation from repeated birth and death. I want only to stay among all the living entities and suffer all distresses on their behalf, so that they may be freed from suffering.”
hinduism.explanation: Rantideva, having given away his last food and water, prays only to share and relieve the sufferings of all beings.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's nayanudaiyaan, his only real want is the ability to relieve others.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on caring only about others' relief; framed devotionally.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says what counts is the willing heart; gifts are judged by what a person has, not by what they lack.
christianity.tie_back: Both locate generosity in the inner disposition that persists when means run out.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on the willing mind; does not describe the pain of being unable to give.

islam.quote_or_event: “Every Muslim has to give in charity.” The people asked, “O Allah's Prophet! If someone has nothing to give, what will he do?” He said, “He should work with his hands and benefit himself and also give in charity (from what he earns).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that even someone with nothing must find a way to give — by working, helping the needy, or doing good deeds.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats the inability to give as a problem the good person must still address.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on the continuing drive to give when one has nothing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone who gives a peruta to a poor person receives six blessings, and whoever consoles him with words of comfort and encouragement receives eleven blessings.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yitzhak teaches that comforting the poor with words is even greater than giving money.
judaism.tie_back: Offers the person without means a way to still do good, answering the Kural's anguish of inability.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 9b (Sefaria, William Davidson ed.)
judaism._accuracy_note: Related but not identical: provides an alternative to material giving rather than describing its absence as poverty.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sasa Jataka, the Bodhisatta born as a hare eats only grass and reflects that he has no oil, rice, or beans to give any beggar who might come; when Sakka arrives disguised as a hungry brahmin, the hare offers his own body by leaping into the fire.
buddhism.explanation: The hare's one concern is that he lacks anything fit to give a hungry guest, so he gives himself.
buddhism.tie_back: Dramatises the Kural's idea that a kind being's true poverty is the inability to give.
buddhism.source: Jataka No. 316, Sasa Jataka (trans. H. T. Francis and R. A. Neil, ed. E. B. Cowell)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the concern at having nothing to give; the story moves straight to total self-sacrifice rather than lament.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor old couple, welcome disguised Zeus and Hermes with the little they have and even try to kill their only goose to feed them.
greek_mythology.explanation: The couple's poverty does not stop them; they strain to give more than they have.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows the ache of the kind-hearted to give despite want, as in the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best: generosity in poverty, but not a reflection on what poverty means to the giver.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is not, therefore, the thing which is done or given, but the spirit in which it is done or given, that must be considered, because a benefit exists, not in that which is done or given, but in the mind of the doer or giver.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that a benefit lies in the giver's intention, not in the material gift.
philosophy.tie_back: Supports the Kural's view that the benefactor's identity lies in the will to give, which persists even without means.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Conceptual parallel; Seneca does not speak of the pain of being unable to give.

kurals.tamil:
ஒப்புரவி னால்வரும் கேடெனின் அஃதொருவன்
விற்றுக்கோள் தக்க துடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Oppuravi naalvarum kedenin aqdhoruvan
Vitrukkol thakka thudaiththu.
kurals.meaning: If someone says that helping others will lead to ruin, then that ruin is worth buying even at the price of selling oneself.
kurals.elementary: Some people say, ‘If you keep giving, you will end up with nothing!’ This kural answers: even if that happens, it is worth it — being someone who helps is worth more than anything you could lose.
kurals.university: The closing couplet answers a prudential objection: oppuravu may lead to kedu, material loss. Valluvar's reply is deliberately extreme — such loss is worth acquiring by selling oneself — and Parimelazhagar notes the logic: nothing is normally bought by selling oneself, so this loss is valued above everything, because it yields lasting renown; hence ‘ruin through oppuravu is not ruin.’ Manakkudavar reframes it as a trade in which one thing is sold to buy a greater, so the apparent loss should be counted as gain. The hyperbole caps the chapter's argument: from rain (211) through wealth (212-217) and poverty (218-219) to self-sacrifice (220), oppuravu is presented as a value that no calculation of self-interest can outweigh.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra, to honour his promise of a gift to the sage Vishvamitra, gives away his kingdom, sells his wife and son, and finally sells himself into servitude at a cremation ground.
hinduism.explanation: In the Markandeya Purana, Harishchandra literally sells himself rather than go back on his pledged gift, and is ultimately exalted by the gods.
hinduism.tie_back: A literal enactment of the Kural's ‘worth buying by selling oneself.’
hinduism.source: Markandeya Purana, Harishchandra legend (chs. 7–8), as summarised in secondary sources
hinduism._accuracy_note: Striking image match (selling oneself); Harishchandra's motive is truthfulness to a promise rather than general social beneficence.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Jesus said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells a rich young man to sell everything he owns and give to the poor.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural's verdict that material ruin for the sake of others is a worthwhile exchange.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on accepting loss for the poor; motivated by discipleship and heavenly treasure.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he who sells himself, seeking means to the approval of Allah. And Allah is kind to [His] servants.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises the one who ‘sells himself’ — gives up his very self — to seek God's pleasure.
islam.tie_back: Uses the same language of selling oneself as the Kural for a supremely worthwhile sacrifice.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbal parallel is striking; the verse concerns devotion to God rather than specifically helping others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In Usha the Sages instituted that one who dispenses his money to charity should not dispense more than one-fifth ... lest he render himself destitute and need the help of other people.”
judaism.explanation: The rabbis limited charitable giving to a fifth of one's assets so that the giver would not become dependent on others.
judaism.tie_back: An honest contrast: Jewish law praises charity but deliberately guards against the self-ruin the Kural welcomes.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 50a (Sefaria, William Davidson ed.)
judaism._accuracy_note: Contrasting view included for honesty; shares high esteem for giving but rejects impoverishing oneself.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If it so happens that, when a disciple of the noble ones obtains these five benefits from wealth, his wealth goes to depletion, the thought occurs to him, ‘Even though my wealth has gone to depletion, I have obtained the five benefits that can be obtained from wealth,’ and he feels no remorse.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that if wealth runs out because it was used well — for family, friends, guests, and the virtuous — the wise feel no regret.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats loss that comes from good use of wealth as no real loss.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.41, Adiya Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on accepting depletion without remorse; less hyperbolic than ‘selling oneself.’

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Prometheus steals fire from the gods and gives it to humankind, and Zeus punishes him by chaining him to a rock where an eagle eats his liver each day.
greek_mythology.explanation: Prometheus accepts terrible suffering as the price of benefiting humanity.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Embodies the Kural's idea that ruin incurred for others' good is worth bearing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match on self-ruin for others' benefit; Prometheus acts by theft and defiance rather than civic duty.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I should not have neglected all my own concerns or patiently seen the neglect of them during all these years, and have been doing yours ... And I have a sufficient witness to the truth of what I say—my poverty.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells the jury that he neglected his own affairs to serve Athens, and his poverty proves it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's benefactor, Socrates accepts material ruin as the price of serving others.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good match on accepting poverty for public service; his ‘service’ is philosophical exhortation, not material aid.
